sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text:
Information:
You must tell the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA) if you're fainting regularly as it could affect your ability to drive.
Find out how to tell the DVLA about fainting (syncope) or blackouts on GOV.UK
You must not drive if your GP has referred you to a specialist and you are waiting to be assessed.

headings.text: Things you can do to prevent fainting

sections.text:
Things you can do to prevent fainting
If you feel like you're about to faint, try to:
lie down with your legs raised – if you cannot do this, then sit with your head lowered between your knees
drink some water
cross your legs while standing up or rock up and down on your toes
clench your fists

sections.heading: If you see someone faint
sections.text:
If you see someone faint
If you're with someone who has fainted, try to keep calm.
First, check if they’re responding by gently shaking their shoulders and asking them loudly if they’re OK. If they do not respond, shout for help, and gently tilt back their head and lift their chin to help them breathe more easily.
Check if they’re breathing by listening for at least 10 seconds. If they’re breathing normally, lay them on their back and raise their legs.
If they’re pregnant (especially if they’re more than 28 weeks pregnant), it’s better to lay them on their side.
Usually, the person who has fainted will wake up within 30 seconds.
